clue.text: Margery's brother gets the bird?

definitions.meaning: in the nursery rhyme See-Saw Margery Daw, Jacky is the boy beside Margery, so he is a Daw too
a small grey-naped crow of the family Corvidae

explanation.surface: A sister watches her sibling get jeered off stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets the bird' reads as the idiom for being booed; here it simply joins the two definitions. See-Saw Margery Daw is an English nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme boy Jack Daw shares his name with the small crow, so both readings land on one word.

clue.text: Stock-dealer at work

parts.note: an old Stock Exchange dealer who traded shares, and also one who does odd jobs for pay

explanation.surface: A trader busy on the exchange floor.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1986 a jobber on the London Stock Exchange dealt in shares with brokers; the word also means a pieceworker who takes jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer who bought and sold shares on the London exchange, and a worker taking piecework.

clue.text: VAT once adapted to foreign exchange

indicators.note: something adapted is altered to suit, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An old sales tax is converted for overseas currency.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is value added tax, the British sales tax. 'Adapted' rearranges VAT ONCE; 'to' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This small coin, a hundredth of a peso or escudo, is money from abroad.

clue.text: Match of the Evening seen on board

definitions.text: Match of the Evening seen on board

parts.words: Match of the Evening seen on board
parts.note: a matching set of plates for the evening meal laid out on the table, board being an old word for table

explanation.surface: A football fixture shown on television one evening.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a televised football match, but 'match' means a matching set and 'board' is the table.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching collection of crockery for serving the evening meal.

clue.text: Aquatic instruction in the river?

definitions.meaning: a series of lessons in the water, such as swimming classes
a stream or channel along which water flows

explanation.surface: Swimming lessons are being held in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: A channel for flowing water, read playfully as lessons in the water.

clue.text: Crude, eh ? Getting twisted and outwitted at cards

indicators.note: being twisted out of shape tells us to rework the letters of the two words before it

explanation.surface: A rough card player is beaten and grumbles about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting twisted' rearranges CRUDE and EH together. Euchre is a trick-taking card game; to be euchred is to be beaten at it, and more widely to be outwitted.
explanation.definitionFit: Euchre is a card game, and being beaten or outplayed in it gives the verb.

clue.text: Printing units currently found in Germany

definitions.meaning: an em is a printer's measure of width
a river in north-west Germany, whose current flows to the North Sea

explanation.surface: Printing presses are now located in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currently' looks like 'at present' but refers to a river's current.
explanation.definitionFit: The printer's measure in the plural, and a north German river, share one spelling.

clue.text: The rent man was in the conspiracy

definitions.text: The rent man was in the conspiracy

parts.words: The rent man was in the conspiracy
parts.note: in Julius Caesar, Antony shows the cut made in Caesar's cloak by one conspirator's dagger

explanation.surface: The landlord's collector was part of the plot.
explanation.walkthrough: Antony: 'See what a rent the envious Casca made.' A rent is a tear, not a payment.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the assassins of Julius Caesar, who struck the first blow.

clue.text: An outstanding work of art

parts.note: sculpture whose figures literally stand out from a flat background

explanation.surface: A masterpiece of exceptional quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Relief carving projects from its background, so it is literally standing out.

clue.text: He settles his disputes in a man to man fashion

definitions.text: He settles his disputes in a man to man fashion

parts.words: He settles his disputes in a man to man fashion
parts.note: one who fights single combat with pistols or swords to settle honour

explanation.surface: A frank fellow resolves arguments face to face.
explanation.definitionFit: A fighter in formal single combat, the old way to resolve a matter of honour.

clue.text: Financial profit from riverside songsters?

parts.note: paper money read whimsically as the songs of birds perched on the shore of a river

explanation.surface: Birds singing by the water are somehow earning money.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper currency is money in hand, and the notes of birds on a river's edge give the playful second reading.

clue.text: Hail, doing lip service

definitions.meaning: the Latin greeting used in English as an exclamation of welcome
an ointment for chapped lips literally serves the lips

explanation.surface: A politician greets everyone while saying only what they want to hear.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin 'salve' is a greeting, and a lip ointment works on the mouth, so the word covers both.

clue.text: Early start not in time to raise one's spirits

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, here taken from the word Early

parts.note: arriving after the due hour means being late

explanation.surface: Getting up early but still running behind does not cheer anyone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early start' looks like one phrase meaning dawn, but it gives just the E of Early.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate someone is to make them joyful, lifting their mood.

clue.text: Excel at Try-Your-Strength machine — stir your memory?

definitions.meaning: at a fairground high striker, hitting hard enough sends the weight up to sound a bell at the top
the idiom for something seeming familiar

explanation.surface: A fairground strongman's feat jogs a forgotten memory.
explanation.walkthrough: A Try-Your-Strength machine is a fairground attraction: hit the pad with a mallet and a puck flies up a tower towards a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking the fairground bell is top marks, and the same phrase is the idiom for sounding familiar.

clue.text: Cheap theatre juke-box?

definitions.meaning: an early American cinema charging a five-cent coin for entry

explanation.surface: A low-cost theatre plays music from a coin machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Named from the five-cent coin, the word covered both early cinemas and coin-slot music players.

clue.text: Where party-lines frequently get crossed

parts.note: the British lower chamber, where members cross the floor between the opposing party benches and argue across the divide

explanation.surface: A telephone exchange where shared lines keep tangling.
explanation.walkthrough: A party line is also a shared telephone line, which is what the surface suggests. In the Westminster chamber, the opposing benches face each other across the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: The elected chamber of the UK Parliament seats rival parties facing each other, and members argue across that floor.

clue.text: Mum is embracing Jolson for silks, satins, etc

parts.note: mater is Latin for mother, used as old British slang for mum

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the word is wraps around the singer's first name

parts.note: Al Jolson, the American singer and actor

explanation.surface: Mother hugs a singer while picking out fine fabrics.
explanation.definitionFit: Silks and satins are examples of fabrics or cloths.

clue.text: Blackleg promises to pay for plant

parts.note: a scab is a strike-breaker
IOUs are written promises to pay a debt

explanation.surface: A strike-breaker signs IOUs to buy a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackleg is British for a worker who breaks a strike. 'For' joins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild flower of the teasel family, with pincushion heads of blue or lilac blooms.

clue.text: Get no nice fruit in exchange for imitation.

indicators.note: the letters are exchanged among themselves, swapping places to make a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone refuses a disappointing piece of fruit and asks for a replacement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In exchange for' reads as a trade; 'in exchange' rearranges GET NO NICE FRUIT and 'for' joins it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Counterfeiting is the making of fakes, copying banknotes or goods.

clue.text: Break into an even run to upset one's opponent

indicators.note: breaking something into pieces scrambles it, so the letters of the two words are reordered

explanation.surface: A runner surges into a steady pace to rattle a rival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break into' reads as starting to run, but it rearranges EVEN RUN; 'an' and 'to' join.
explanation.definitionFit: To shake someone's nerve is to disturb and fluster them.

clue.text: Profit-making fence ?

definitions.meaning: to net is to clear as profit
mesh of wire or cord used as a barrier

explanation.surface: A receiver of stolen goods makes a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: A fence is also a receiver of stolen goods, which the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: Clearing money after costs, and a barrier of mesh, share one word.

clue.text: What kings and queens! What heavenly gates!

definitions.meaning: London costermongers' ... kings and queens wear clothes covered with buttons of mother-of-pearl
heaven's entrance is traditionally the ... gates

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims at royal splendour and the gates of paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London charity figures whose costumes are sewn with mother-of-pearl buttons.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the button-covered London street royalty and heaven's gates take this adjective meaning nacreous.

clue.text: Spanish highwayman; and in "a dance-jacket!

indicators.note: the word and is placed in the middle of the dance and garment

parts.note: a bolero is both a Spanish dance and a short open jacket

explanation.surface: A Spanish bandit dances about in a short jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: The bolero is both a lively Spanish dance and a short open jacket, so one word fits the hyphenated pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Bandolero is the Spanish word for a bandit or robber of travellers.

clue.text: Decoration of gold on red mount

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry

indicators.note: to mount is to go up, so the word red is read upwards

explanation.surface: A gold medal is displayed on a red backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mount' looks like a backing for a medal; in a down clue it turns RED upwards to give DER.
explanation.definitionFit: An order is an honour or insignia, such as the Order of the Garter.

clue.text: What, sailor, back so early ?

indicators.note: going back means the words for what and sailor are read in the opposite direction

parts.note: eh? is a cry of 'what?'
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: Someone is surprised to see a seaman returning so soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' turns EH + TAR around. Rathe is an archaic or poetic word for early, as in Milton's 'rathe primrose'.
explanation.definitionFit: This old poetic adjective means coming before the usual time, as of flowers blooming soon in spring.

clue.text: Wielded blades in East Road riot

indicators.note: a riot throws everything into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Knives were brandished during a street disturbance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wielded blades' suggests knives; the blades are of oars. 'Riot' rearranges E + ROAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A rowing oar ends in a flat blade, so those who pulled them through the water oared.

clue.text: The young one was a darling

definitions.text: The young one was a darling

parts.words: The young one was a darling
parts.note: Bonnie Prince Charlie was called the Young Pretender's title in French style, and the Jacobite song calls him my darling

explanation.surface: Someone recalls a child who was sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Edward Stuart was known as the Young Chevalier, and the Jacobite song 'Charlie is my darling' is about him.
explanation.definitionFit: A French title for a knight or gallant, given to the Stuart claimant.

clue.text: Champion of Scotland Yard ?

definitions.meaning: El ..., the Castilian hero Rodrigo Díaz
the Criminal Investigation Department of London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Who is Scotland Yard's star detective?
explanation.walkthrough: Scotland Yard is the headquarters of London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish hero El Cid, and the detective branch of the Metropolitan Police.

clue.text: Clipped ear in the outhouse!

indicators.note: the ear is placed in the middle of the outhouse

parts.note: a shed is a small outbuilding

explanation.surface: Someone got a clip round the ear out in the shed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clipped ear' suggests a cuff on the head; 'clipped' is the definition, cut as wool from sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: Shears cut wool or hair, so something shorn or trimmed has been clipped.

clue.text: Flair the poet John had with flowers

parts.note: a nose for something is a natural talent or instinct
John Gay, eighteenth-century poet and author of The Beggar's Opera

explanation.surface: An eighteenth-century poet had a gift for arranging blooms.
explanation.definitionFit: A small posy is a little bunch of blooms.
